item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Petition opposing Hakeem Jeffries as US House Speaker passes one million signatures
item.description:
Petition opposing Hakeem Jeffries as US House Speaker passes one million signatures

Submitted by Mounira Elsamra on Tue, 11/10/2026 - 19:08
Jeffries is expected to become the first Black speaker when the new Congress convenes in January
US House of Representatives Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks during a press conference at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on 9 November 2026 (Jim Watson/AFP)
Off

More than a million people have signed a petition urging Democrats to reject Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the US House of Representatives, as growing opposition to his leadership puts his support for Israel and US foreign policy under renewed scrutiny.

Jeffries, who currently leads the House Democrats, is expected to become the first Black speaker when the new Congress convenes in January, after the Democrats' sweeping midterm victories on 3 November.

But Jeffries is not the speaker-elect yet. He confirmed his candidacy last week, but his colleagues must elect him later this month. Jeffries stands currently uncontested, with no other Democratic lawmaker throwing their hat in the ring for the position.

While no one in the party has come forward to run against Jeffries, several newly elected lawmakers have voiced reservations about his policy positions, casting doubt on whether or not they will endorse him.

Some voters and influencers have mobilised, with dozens of viral videos urging citizens to call their representatives and sign the petition against Jeffries. 

“We believe the Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” says the petition put forward by social media influencer Nicole Whitted.  

The petition calls on representatives to examine Jeffries' public record, policy positions, campaign donor record, and leadership. 

'It’s not enough to criticise the war we need to defund it'

- Etan Mabourakh, National Iranian American Council

An Economist/YouGov poll published last month found that Jeffries had just a 26 percent approval rating among registered voters. 

Critics say that one reason Jeffries' popularity has taken a hit is that he is an avid supporter of Israel.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) ranks among his top campaign-financing contributors. 

Israel's favourability among Americans has plummeted in recent years, according to a poll from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, which shows Israel has its lowest favourability since 1978. 

According to Track AIPAC, Jeffries has taken $1.5m in donations from the pro-Israel lobbying group. Aipac took to social media platform X to congratulate Jeffries on his win.

A resurfaced clip of Jeffries speaking at a United Jewish Appeal event where he says “Israel today, Israel tomorrow, Israel forever” is making the rounds online, with influencers urging people to call their representatives.

New Yorkers protest against Jeffries

On Monday, Brooklyn For Peace held a rally outside of Jeffries' office in New York City's Brooklyn borough.

Dozens of protesters gathered holding signs that read “Stop weapons to Israel” and chanting “hey hey, ho ho, this genocide has got to go”, in reference to the war on Gaza, where over 74,500 Palestinians have been killed. 

The organisers handed a letter to one of the lawmaker’s staffers, urging Jeffries to oppose all further funding for the war on Iran, oppose supplying weapons to Israel, block and cut Trump’s Pentagon war budget, and abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), among other demands. 

Brooklyn for Peace chair Charlotte Phillips had a message for Jeffries saying, “We need you to stand up and take action to protect us and our children from what's happening now, which is of such tremendous harm to us future generations and to our entire community.”

Etan Mabourakh, the group's executive director, says Jeffries’ foreign policy stance is making him unpopular with constituents.

“Anyone seeking to lead not just the Democratic Party but the American people must back broadly popular and urgent positions: defunding the illegal war on Iran, blocking weapons used in war crimes by the Israeli government, blocking the proposed merger of the US and Israeli militaries, and welcoming immigrants and abolishing ICE.”  

Jeffries has previously called the Iran war illegal and unconstitutional, but Mabourakh says those words are not enough. 

“It’s not enough to criticise the war; we need to defund it.” 

Among the protesters was New York resident Mitty Owens, who says Jeffries represents “profit over people and Israel over the US”.

Owens believes that Jeffries is standing on the wrong side of history. 

“Holocaust experts and academics say this is genocide. It’s obvious that Israel targets and kills civilians, aid workers, and journalists. There's no excuse whatsoever why a single dollar more should be going to Israel with no conditions whatsoever.”  

He blames lobbying groups for the reason politicians like Jeffries have not stood against Israel. 

Owens is calling for a new Democratic leader in the House, saying that Jeffries has “lost his way”, going so far as to call him Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu's puppet.

“Why is he veering so far from what he knows is right? Because of the level of money that's in there, he's listening to Aipac and following corporate interests over listening to constituents”.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] US House Democrat leader Jeffries will retain position despite opposition, sources say
item.description:
US House Democrat leader Jeffries will retain position despite opposition, sources say

Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Tue, 11/10/2026 - 19:15
In the Senate, unless progressive-backed Chris Van Hollen formally steps up to unite the ranks as a challenger, Chuck Schumer will likely win
The leader of the House Democrats, New York Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, right, speaks to reporters alongside the leader of the Senate Democrats, New York Senator Chuck Schumer, on the steps of the US Senate on 21 May 2026 in Washington, DC (Win McNamee/Getty Images via AFP)
Off

The top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, is all but certain to become the next Speaker of the House, despite dissatisfaction among some freshman lawmakers and their progressive colleagues in the chamber, sources have told Middle East Eye. 

There simply is no alternative leader in the running. 

"It's a cost to go against someone who will eventually be the leader of the caucus. There's not enough people who are willing to do that," one source said. 

This comes as many voters have expressed their desire to see Jeffries vacate the position, accusing him of being out of step with the party's growing leftist progressive wing, which wants to see money out of politics, and a stop to the transfer of weapons to Israel. 

New lawmakers are looking to work with him instead, three sources familiar with the internal process on Capitol Hill confirmed to MEE. 

The 56-year-old Jeffries is backed by pro-Israel lobbying groups and has made it clear he is an avowed protector of Israel. He has also received substantial financial support from a litany of big corporations, including tech and weapons manufacturers. 

Perhaps most importantly, his candidacy in his New York district and his leadership bid were endorsed by progressive kingmaker and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani - much to the chagrin of Mamdani's own supporters.

Petition opposing Hakeem Jeffries as US House Speaker passes one million signatures
Read More »

Mamdani is largely credited with setting off a wave of young Democratic Socialists launching campaigns for office. 

Just before the 3 November midterm elections, Redbox Research's polling showed only 19 percent of Democratic voters want to keep Jeffries as their leader in Congress.

A Change.org petition last week already had one million signatures calling for him to step aside. 

The Speaker of the House is second in line to the US presidency, after the vice president. Jeffries, in particular, would also become the first Black lawmaker to ever assume the role. 

"I would suspect most Democrats will think twice about about blocking that historic achievement - even if they have other concerns about Jeffries," Chris Edelson, a constitutional scholar and political science lecturer at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst, told MEE on Tuesday.

'Undecided'

The vote, which is done through secret ballot, is set for next week. The 120th Congress will be sworn in on 3 January 2027. 

Speaking to reporters during their new member onboarding session this week, some of the most progressive, pro-Palestine, political novices made it clear they are willing to work with anyone who shares their goal of delivering for voters - even though they were specifically asked about whether they would back Jeffries.

"This was a historic class [of new lawmakers], one that has a lot of firsts," Colorado Representative-elect Melat Kiros said.

"We might have different ideas about how to accomplish certain things, but we all agree that we have to reduce costs for families. We all agree that we have to root out corruption in government. We all agree that our foreign policy has to actually reflect our values. In order for us to be able to do that, we need an agenda that's bold enough to meet that vision," she said.

JD Vance blames Iran war and support for Israel for failure in US mid-term elections
Read More »

"And so what we're demanding is an agenda. It's not about the individual. It's about what kind of priorities, what kind of floor votes, what kind of plan do we have to actually fight."

New Jersey Representative-elect Adam Hamawy maintained the group is "undecided". 

"We're not going to rubber stamp anything. We want to sit and have a conversation about the issues and what's the plan going forward. And I think that's what the American people elected us to do, is to have these conversations," he said. 

Ohio Representative-elect Don Leonard, however, posted a video on Instagram on Monday, making it clear he'd been told there would be consequences for not voting for Jeffries.

"I met with... senior members of the Democratic House, who told me in no uncertain terms that the decision as to whether or not I support Jeffries, regardless of his willingness to speak with me and meet the interests of my constituents on a couple of key issues... would basically mean both making my life a living hell for the next two years here in Washington, as well as being sure to lose my election in two years," he said. 

Those key issues, he explained, were getting corporate money out of politics, and ending US support for Israel and its wars in the region. 

"The big 'D' Democratic Party needs some little 'd' democracy," Leonard added. 

On Tuesday, Republicans came together to declare Trump loyalist and Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan as their leader in the House for the next session, and to keep South Dakota Senator John Thune as the minority leader in the Senate.

Senate tussle

Indeed, ensuring that party members get in line is, in effect, the job of the leader.

Building personal relationships is critical in the corridors of power, Neil Sroka, a former progressive strategist, told MEE on Tuesday.

"It's not just ideological [matters] that drive decision-making behind who's a [Senate] Majority Leader and who's a Speaker of the House. There are regional concerns, there are state delegation concerns, and so the politics of it are very complicated, and I don't envy any member of Congress or a member of the US Senate who are trying to figure out how to navigate those complicated waters, and especially in an ideologically complicated result as in this election."

If someone's leadership bid is potentially threatened, it could be the top Democrat in the Senate, the 75-year-old Chuck Schumer, sources told MEE. At the very least, his support base would be eroded even if he retains his post, and he would have to make room for the left-wing flank to bring their issues to the floor.

He is even more unpopular among Democratic voters than Jeffries, polling at just 11 percent favourability. 

'Schumer’s foreign policy record is a serious liability for his continued leadership'

- Cavan Kharrazian, senior policy adviser, Demand Progress

The New York senator is also backed by corporate interests and is a staunch supporter of Israel, as well as a hawk on Iran, even if he didn't like the way President Donald Trump himself carried out a seemingly endless war.

"Politics matters to some extent, but it also matters who a senator is going to see in the Senate gym," Sroka explained. "That's what we recalled back from the 2018 race - even though there might have been some agita about Leader Schumer and whether or not he was really in line with the rest of the Senate, he had everyone on speed dial. Everyone knew him really well, and it was very hard to step outside of that lane."

On Tuesday, anti-war activists from Code Pink, among other groups, staged a protest outside Schumer's office after being locked out by his staff, they said. 

They were specifically protesting against the $1.5 trillion budget requested by the Trump administration for the Department of War, which will have to go through the Senate.

The bill also includes a provision that would permanently integrate US and Israeli military tech advancements in a way that would - as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu put it - turn Israel from a foreign aid recipient to a full-scale partner. 

Only one senator with some limited backing to be speaker has emerged as a vocal advocate of such a move: Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen. He is perhaps the Senate's most visible progressive voice on foreign policy, after Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders. 

Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has already said for months he would like to see Van Hollen elected as the top Democrat in the Senate, even though the senator had not shown interest in the position.

"I have said that I am in listening mode," Van Hollen told a reporter on Capitol Hill this week. "There are clearly lots of people around the country, and a number of our members, quite a few of our members, who want to have this discussion, and so I'm in active listening mode... I haven't closed the door."

Cavan Kharrazian, a senior policy adviser with the group Demand Progress, told MEE that Schumer's record comes into sharper focus now that Van Hollen has emerged as a possibility. 

"Van Hollen has been at the forefront in the Senate of challenging unconditional support for Israel and has made clear he will oppose funding legislation in the lame duck [session]," he said. "That puts real pressure on Schumer to take a firm stand against war funding... and explain how he can lead his caucus in the direction voters are demanding after spending so much of his career resisting it."

Schumer has long been criticised as being too soft on Trump since his first term from 2016-2020, and the backlash against the current administration in the midterm elections has, if anything, shown that Democrats want fighters to represent them.

“Schumer’s foreign policy record is a serious liability for his continued leadership," Kharrazian said. "The midterms underscored the need for leaders who will confront Trump’s reckless wars and forge a new foreign policy grounded in diplomacy, human rights, and people’s needs at home," Kharrazian added.

"The UN climate summit is a good opportunity to discuss the actions the US and Israel have taken to damage the environment in Iran and the region," Pezeshkian said.

  • The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said it received the report of an incident involving a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz. It added that the status of the crew, the extent of any damage and the environmental impact were not yet known.

A senior intelligence official in the ​Trump administration warned that Tehran has increased efforts to target US personnel.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Trump cannot freeze the Iran war on his own terms
item.description:
Trump cannot freeze the Iran war on his own terms

Submitted by Shahir Shahidsaless on Tue, 11/10/2026 - 16:03
The US president can choose not to start another all-out conflict - but he cannot keep Tehran bleeding indefinitely
An Iranian woman holds up a portrait of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, in front of an anti-Trump billboard in Tehran, on 3 November 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
Off

On Monday, US President Donald Trump appeared to rule out another major offensive against Iran, at least for now. After speaking with Qatar’s prime minister, he said Washington was maintaining the “status quo”.

In a Truth Social post, he said Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait favoured continuing the naval blockade and “Operation Iron Gate”. Further escalation was “quite unlikely”, he suggested, although US forces remained “locked and loaded”.

Days earlier, Trump had been considering new strikes. Now he appears to favour keeping Iran under economic and military pressure without risking another major war. 

The flaw is obvious: Washington can choose to maintain a blockade. It cannot decide how long Tehran will tolerate it.

Also on Monday, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, called Washington a “desperate gambler”, denounced reports of “imaginary talks”, and demanded that the US “surrender” to Iran’s conditions. 

Trump sees a manageable stalemate; Tehran sees an unacceptable siege.

For the Islamic Republic, this confrontation is existential. An indefinite blockade would inflict mounting economic damage, without guaranteeing relief or protection from another attack. Meanwhile, Gulf producers continue selling whatever oil they can export. Iran is left bleeding while others continue business.

Asymmetric warfare

Falling prices compound Tehran’s predicament: Brent crude plunged six percent on Monday, diminishing the global economic pressure that had helped Iran deter Washington. Tehran has little incentive to let its adversaries enjoy lower energy prices while its own economy remains strangled.

Iran could therefore intensify disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, target shipping, or conduct limited but damaging attacks against regional energy facilities. Such escalation follows a pattern already visible: Reuters reported continuing tanker attacks and limited US strikes, even as Trump advocated the status quo.

The logic of asymmetric warfare is different. Iran need not defeat the US military. It needs only to impose costs sufficiently punishing to overcome Washington’s will to sustain the war.

Trump may hope that sustained pressure will force Tehran to concede. But Iran's leaders could instead escalate to make the blockade intolerable

Above all, Tehran wants to establish that another attack cannot occur without prolonged, enormous economic losses. That deterrent, not battlefield parity, is central to its strategy.

Iranian escalation could force Trump to respond. Limited US strikes will not compel Tehran’s capitulation, as two wars have already demonstrated. An all-out offensive, meanwhile, could trigger the very regional catastrophe he hopes to avoid.

The US can devastate Iranian targets, but destruction does not guarantee surrender. An assessment of six military options by the Center for Strategic and International Studies think-tank underscores the dilemma. Limited strikes may achieve little; broader bombing invites retaliation; securing enriched uranium could require a dangerous ground operation; and regime change offers no guarantee of a stable successor.

Previous attacks damaged Iran’s capabilities without compelling Tehran to surrender its uranium, accept Washington’s demands, or reopen Hormuz on American terms. For leaders who believe the regime’s survival is at stake, further punishment may strengthen the determination to resist.

Structural vulnerability 

A slew of analysts suggest Trump might try to bury his electoral defeat beneath a massive offensive before the Democratic Congress convenes on 3 January.

David Sanger, White House correspondent for the New York Times, notes that lame-duck presidents sometimes turn to military power to demonstrate undiminished authority, recalling former President George W Bush’s escalation in Iraq after the 2006 Republican defeat. 

The argument is that an offensive before 3 January could create a military fait accompli, making incoming lawmakers reluctant to interrupt a war already under way. But that is like an accountant meticulously entering prospective profits while leaving the losses column blank.

Iran has warned that renewed attacks could bring retaliation against Gulf energy infrastructure, data centres and undersea cables. Conflict monitor ACLED documented at least 172 attacks on nonmilitary infrastructure across six Gulf monarchies between 28 February and 30 July, nearly half involving energy facilities. 

A Congressional Research Service report recorded more than 6,700 drones and missiles fired at Gulf states by 17 May, while industry estimates placed energy-infrastructure damage above $25bn by early April.

The vulnerability is structural. Destroy one critical component, and a far larger network can be crippled; alternative export routes are vulnerable too. Damaged liquified natural-gas (LNG) installations may take years to restore, while attacks on Gulf production could jeopardise exports and drive crude above $130 a barrel, according to one analysis.

The warning from Saudi Aramco itself is even more sobering. Early last month, CEO Amin Nasser said the crisis had already removed nearly three billion barrels of gross oil supply. “Until Hormuz fully re-opens and confidence returns, the crude reality is that pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify.” He was referring not only to crude oil, but also to refined products, such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.

This is precisely why Gulf governments fear paying for decisions made in Washington. A military fait accompli could produce an economic fait accompli of its own. Tehran’s aim would be to make that prospect so credible that Washington could not contemplate another offensive without reckoning with the lasting damage.

Congress' power of the purse

Trump’s military authority does not give him unlimited money to sustain a war. The distinction matters: a president may order operations using existing authority and resources, but Congress controls future appropriations and can legislate restrictions on how even previously appropriated money is spent. 

The federal funding extension expires on 11 December, creating a confrontation over government spending. Democrats can withhold support for a new extension unless it contains restrictions on funding offensive operations against Iran. 

The warning is no longer abstract. Senator Chris Van Hollen declared: “I’m not planning to vote for anything that provides any funding to fuel the war in Iran.” He added that if Trump chooses to shut down the federal government to continue the war, the responsibility would fall on the president alone.

Separately, Republicans’ proposed $73bn defence-funding package is only a budget blueprint, not appropriated war funding. The House approved the resolution 216-214; a single Republican switching sides would have defeated it. 

Iran war: Trump can continue the same failed policies - or shape a historic legacy
Read More »

Any actual funding measure must still pass Congress. Republican defections over Iran war powers show that party unity cannot be assumed, particularly after the midterms. Four House Republicans and four Republican senators broke ranks in June; seven House Republicans supported a war-powers resolution in September.

Those votes did not themselves stop the war, but they exposed the fragility of Trump’s congressional backing.

Congress has wielded its financial power before, during the Vietnam War. In 1973, it prohibited the use of funds, including money already appropriated, for US combat operations after 15 August. Then-president Richard Nixon signed the legislation; the bombing of Cambodia ended on that date.

Trump’s weakened position matters. NBC’s national exit poll found that 63 percent of voters said the decision to attack Iran was wrong. Moreover, an AP-NORC poll found that seven in 10 registered voters want Congress to prioritise ending the war, which it never authorised.

An economic shock from a new war would hit a president already punished at the ballot box.

Trump may hope that sustained pressure will force Tehran to concede. But Iran’s leaders could instead escalate to make the blockade intolerable, increasing the risk of miscalculation and an expanding conflict. The US could respond with limited attacks that fail to settle anything, or a larger war whose economic and political costs could devastate Trump’s presidency.

Neither outcome resolves the nuclear dispute. A prolonged siege risks renewed war and, eventually, a more dangerous confrontation. The alternative is a negotiated compromise, requiring concessions neither side can extract by force.

Trump can choose not to start another all-out war. He cannot choose to keep Iran bleeding indefinitely without a response. The status quo is not an exit strategy.
